strengths: Well-motivated hierarchical agent design that clearly articulates the need for coordinated reasoning-driven search and search-informed reasoning
Strong experimental results across multiple benchmarks (EX-FEVER, HOVER, CHECKWHY) with consistent improvements, particularly on challenging 3-4 hop reasoning
Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating the value of multi-agent design over single-agent baselines and the impact of coordinated training rounds
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 6-9) showing concrete examples of agent coordination and case studies comparing multi-agent vs. single-agent approaches
Thorough experimental documentation including prompt templates, hyperparameters, dataset splits, and implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (GRPO from Shao et al. 2024, tag-based control from Chen et al. 2025, standard RL) without significant methodological advances

Unfair baseline comparisons: HARIS uses Qwen-3 4B while most baselines use GPT-4o (much larger); missing comparison with HARIS using larger models to isolate method contribution from model size effects
Narrow evaluation scope limited to Wikipedia-based datasets with only binary classification (Support/Refute), excluding Neutral and Not Enough Info; no cross-domain or out-of-distribution evaluation
Lacks statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple runs reported; improvements of 0.3-2% on many metrics lack statistical validation

Training data synthesis concerns: search agent training data synthesized with GPT-4o (~10% filtered out) introduces potential bias; limited analysis of synthesis quality and distribution alignment with reasoning agent questions
No analysis of core mechanism: missing quantitative study of search refinement patterns, query quality, or systematic investigation of when/why agents call each other
Absence of failure analysis and error characterization: only positive case studies shown; unclear when method fails or what systematic failure modes exist
High computational barriers (4xH20 + 8xA100 GPUs) and context length limitations (8192 tokens) restrict reproducibility; inference latency not reported

Arbitrary coordinated training design: no justification for alternating vs. joint training; Table 3 shows N=3 and N=1 perform similarly on some metrics; reward values (0, 0.1, 1) lack sensitivity analysis

strengths: Clear problem motivation: The paper effectively articulates and demonstrates why reasoning and information search must be coordinated rather than decomposed statically, with compelling examples like Figure 1.

Technically sound approach: The hierarchical decomposition is well-justified, GRPO training is appropriately applied, and the two-stage coordinated training strategy (foundation + alternating) is novel in this context.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Consistent improvements across three benchmarks (EX-FEVER, HOVER, CHECKWHY) with thorough ablation studies examining single vs. multi-agent design, coordination rounds, and reward metrics.
Strong reproducibility: Detailed prompts, hyperparameters, human evaluation of the LLM-as-a-Judge reward (Cohen's Kappa: 0.81, 93.3% agreement), and clear experimental setup enable reproducibility.
Effective qualitative analysis: Case studies (Figures 6-9) convincingly demonstrate coordinated agent advantages through concrete examples and direct single vs. multi-agent comparisons.
Good generalization: Strong performance on the causally-structured CHECKWHY dataset suggests the approach generalizes beyond training distributions.
weaknesses: Model scale disparity: HARIS uses Qwen3-4B while most baselines use GPT-4o; although Table 5 provides Qwen3-4B baseline comparisons, the core advantage may partly reflect architectural design rather than pure scale. Unclear how HARIS would perform with larger models, limiting assessment of real-world value.

Limited scope: Binary claim classification only (Support/Refute), excluding Neutral or Not Enough Info classes that real-world fact-checking requires. This significantly limits practical applicability.

Search agent training data synthesis concerns: Pseudo ground-truth answers from GPT-4o introduce distributional bias; questions sampled from undertrained reasoning agent H₀ may be unrepresentative; no analysis of how pseudo-label errors propagate through training.

Modest improvements in some cases: HOVER 2-hops shows only 0.59% improvement over Search-o1; no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or power analysis provided despite evaluation on only 500 test samples per dataset.

Oversimplified reward design: Reasoning agent uses coarse binary reward (1/0.1/0) that may provide insufficient learning signal; LLM-as-a-Judge for search agent has known biases and is not robustly evaluated across prompt variations.

Limited novelty in components: GRPO, hierarchical agents, and multi-agent RL are established techniques; main novelty is the application domain plus a relatively straightforward alternating training strategy.
Missing failure analysis: No systematic breakdown of failure modes, cases where extra search hurts performance, or analysis of agent disagreements. Only positive examples shown in case studies.

Prompt engineering dependency: Heavy reliance on carefully crafted domain-specific prompts (Table 8) with no robustness analysis; unclear how sensitive results are to prompt variations or applicability to other fact-checking domains.
Insufficient training set analysis: Only 7,200 examples for RL training; no learning curves or sensitivity studies showing whether performance scales with more data.
Unaddressed computational costs: Training and inference require two models with GRPO, but costs are not compared to baselines, limiting assessment of practical deployment feasibility.
